summary.detailed_summary: The paper scales the LaBraM EEG foundation model by increasing pretraining data across three collections (Quark, Atom, Molecule) and expanding encoder capacity from 5.8M to 1.97B parameters. It employs a neural spectrum tokenizer and masked-code prediction objective to learn representations across 23 diverse downstream tasks. Results show that scaling improves both full fine-tuning and linear probing, with the Atom-L* model outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.61 percentage points in mean balanced accuracy.

headline_results: Atom-L* achieved 59.05% mean balanced accuracy (Full-FT), +3.61 pp over REVE Large
Quark-G achieved 54.33% mean balanced accuracy (LP)

key_points: New EEG foundation model: Scales LaBraM to 1.97B parameters and ~80k hours of data, achieving state-of-the-art mean balanced accuracy of 59.05% on 23 tasks.
Scaling analysis: Reveals that larger encoders benefit more from full fine-tuning than linear probing and that downstream performance can decouple from pretraining loss.
Data efficiency: Shows that broader source coverage (Atom) can outperform larger but less diverse collections (Quark) at matched model sizes.
limitations: Downstream performance can decline even as pretraining loss continues to fall.
Linear probing performance does not consistently guarantee strong full fine-tuning results.
Increasing the size of the language model readout (Qwen3) provided no consistent gain in multitask classification.
Data saturation occurs depending on model capacity, limiting the returns of simply adding more hours.

method.architecture: Neural spectrum tokenizer with scaled encoders (5.8M to 1.97B parameters)
method.finetuning: Full fine-tuning (Full-FT) and Linear Probing (LP)
method.objective: Masked-code prediction
method.pretraining: Distributed training on heterogeneous EEG recordings across three data collections

summary.title: LaBraM at Scale: Scaling Data and Models for EEG Pretraining
summary.unique_contribution: Provides a comprehensive analysis of the scaling laws for EEG foundation models, demonstrating capacity-dependent data saturation and the divergence between linear probing and full fine-tuning performance.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper tests the Platonic Representation Hypothesis by analyzing 14 EEG foundation models across five families using the CineBrain dataset. It introduces 'NICE decodability' as a task-free measure of capability and uses calibrated mKNN and CKA metrics to assess representational alignment. The results show that higher decodability predicts stronger intramodal convergence and global alignment with language models, while parameter count is not a consistent proxy for alignment.

headline_results: Positive correlation between NICE decodability and cross-family alignment (mKNN p=0.003, CKA p=0.007)
No consistent correlation between parameter count and alignment

key_points: Analysis of EEG foundation models: Tests the Platonic Representation Hypothesis to see if models converge on shared representations as they improve.
Capability over scale: Found that alignment correlates with the ability to decode general EEG markers (NICE decodability) rather than model parameter count.
Cross-modal dissociation: Observed strong global alignment with language models for high-capability EEG models, but no consistent local alignment with vision models.
limitations: Small sample size of 14 models from five families.
Limited number of participants (six subjects).
Reliance on a single dataset (CineBrain), limiting generalizability.
Cross-modal neighborhood similarity only modestly exceeded the time-shifted control.

method.architecture: Analysis of 14 frozen EEG models (FEMBA, LUNA, NeuroLM, ST-EEGFormer, REVE) compared with vision and language models.
method.objective: Representational alignment analysis using mKNN (local) and Linear CKA (global) with a cyclic-shift null calibration.
method.pretraining: Models were pretrained on large-scale EEG data as per their original publications.

summary.title: The Platonic Brain: Representational Convergence in EEG Foundation Models
summary.unique_contribution: Demonstrates that representational convergence in EEG foundation models is driven by model capability (NICE decodability) rather than parameter scale.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper explores whether generalist VLMs can interpret EEG visually, emulating the way clinicians inspect EEG patterns, without requiring large-scale EEG-specific pretraining. The authors demonstrate that VLMs like Qwen3-VL perform competitively on clinical tasks (vEpiSet, TUEV, TUAB) and exhibit scaling laws and superior few-shot adaptability compared to specialist EEG foundation models. Evidence shows that the choice of visual rendering, specifically longitudinal bipolar montages, significantly enhances diagnostic performance.

headline_results: Qwen-4B achieved 0.835 balanced accuracy on vEpiSet, outperforming specialist FMs (0.763).

key_points: New EEG foundation model approach: leverages generalist Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to interpret EEG signals as visual patterns.
Shows that VLMs exhibit performance scaling with model size and superior few-shot adaptation compared to specialist EEG-pretrained models.
Achieved state-of-the-art balanced accuracy (0.750) on the TUEV FM-Bench split using Qwen3-VL-8B.
limitations: Naive VLMs lack strong zero-shot capacities on EEG tasks.
Performance is highly dependent on the visual rendering method (e.g., montage type).
Requires fine-tuning for optimal clinical performance.

method.finetuning: LoRA or prediction-head adaptation

summary.unique_contribution: Demonstrates that generalist VLMs can serve as effective EEG foundation models without domain-specific pretraining, exhibiting scaling and few-shot capabilities that specialist EEG models lack.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a geometric hierarchy metric to analyze how EEG foundation models and signal processing features organize trait (subject identity) and state (task) information. The authors find that most embeddings form a macro-trait hierarchy, which negatively correlates with state classification performance. They demonstrate that subject mean-normalization and task-specific fine-tuning can shift this hierarchy toward a macro-state organization, thereby improving BCI performance.

headline_results: Strong negative correlation (Spearman -0.73) between macro-trait hierarchy and state classification accuracy.
Subject mean-normalization improved balanced accuracy by approximately 10%.

key_points: Analysis method for EEG representations: Quantifies the trait-state hierarchy in embeddings to show that subject identity typically dominates task-related signatures.
Evidence of performance bottleneck: Finds a strong negative correlation (Spearman -0.73) between macro-trait hierarchy and state classification accuracy.
Mitigation strategies: Demonstrates that subject mean-normalization and fine-tuning transform embeddings from macro-trait to macro-state hierarchies, improving balanced accuracy by ~10%.
limitations: Current pre-training objectives may inherently bias models toward capturing subject identity over task states.
The magnitude of performance gains from normalization depends on the existing state purity within subjects.
Some tasks show smaller separation between subject and state purity, suggesting task-dependent representation.

method.architecture: Analyzes embeddings from various FMs (BIOT, LaBraM, CBraMod, CSBrain, REVE) and signal processing features.
method.finetuning: Evaluates task-specific fine-tuning and subject mean-normalization to shift the trait-state hierarchy.
method.objective: Uses a Hierarchy Metric (ratio of inter-trait to intra-trait distances) and kNN purity to evaluate representation structure.
method.pretraining: Evaluates models using contrastive and masked reconstruction objectives.

summary.one_liner: Quantifies the dominance of subject-specific 'traits' over task-specific 'states' in EEG embeddings and shows that reducing trait information improves state decoding.
summary.title: Quantifying Trait-State Hierarchy in EEG Foundation Model and Signal Processing Embeddings
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a quantitative hierarchy metric to reveal that EEG foundation models primarily capture subject-specific traits, which hinders state decoding unless mitigated by normalization or fine-tuning.

summary.detailed_summary: The authors propose the EEGDash Corpus, a curated collection of 77 redistributable public EEG datasets totaling over 14,000 hours of recordings. Unlike previous large-scale corpora that rely on non-redistributable clinical archives, this corpus is provided as a gated Hugging Face dataset in a chunked Zarr store. The utility of the corpus is validated by retraining the REVE-Base model from scratch, achieving performance on OpenEEGBench tasks comparable to the original released model.

headline_results: Linear probing score of 0.331 (vs 0.333 released)
Fine-tuning score of 0.273 (vs 0.325 released)

key_points: New EEG benchmark: A training-ready corpus containing 77 public datasets, 14,075 hours of EEG data, and 7,272 subjects.
Provides a standardized Zarr store format and conversion pipeline based on the REVE model's recipe to streamline foundation model pretraining.
Demonstrates viability by retraining REVE-Base from scratch, reaching a 0.331 linear probing score on OpenEEGBench tasks.
limitations: Excludes 12 datasets from the original REVE corpus due to redistribution restrictions.
Excludes datasets recorded at 100 Hz as they fall below the 200 Hz input requirement of the REVE recipe.
Performance of the retrained model is slightly lower than the original released model due to missing clinical data.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a framework to adapt the frozen SleepFM foundation model for precise sleep spindle localization, addressing the resolution loss caused by multi-second token compression. It introduces a parallel local time-frequency branch with a band-structured readout and a localized wavelet synthesis decoder to reconstruct sample-level boundaries. Evaluation on the MODA benchmark shows an event-level F1 of 0.8080 at IoU 0.2, demonstrating that combining local spectral details with pretrained temporal context improves dense event recovery.

headline_results: Event-level F1 of 0.8080 ± 0.0040 at IoU 0.2
Event-level F1 of 0.7766 ± 0.0050 at IoU 0.5

key_points: Method for adapting sleep foundation models: utilizes a frozen SleepFM encoder augmented with a local time-frequency branch for dense spindle localization.
Employs a band-structured readout and localized wavelet synthesis to reconstruct temporal details below the pretrained token scale.
Achieves an event-level F1 of 0.8080 at IoU 0.2 on the MODA benchmark, showing that local spectral information is primary for localization while the FM provides context.
limitations: Performance declines rapidly at stricter IoU thresholds, indicating challenges in very precise boundary alignment.
Relies on a frozen backbone, which may limit the potential for deeper task-specific feature adaptation.
Evaluation is limited to the MODA benchmark.

method.architecture: Frozen SleepFM encoder + local time-frequency branch (Morlet wavelets, SE-module, CNNs) + asymmetric cross-attention + localized wavelet synthesis decoder + TCN refinement.
method.finetuning: Frozen backbone with trainable local pathway and decoder.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper investigates whether adapters that mirror the channel and temporal structure of a pretrained EEG backbone (native adapters) outperform simple token-wise MLP adapters when trainable parameter counts are matched. Using CBraMod and LaBraM backbones across tasks like emotion recognition and sleep staging, the authors find that native adapters show no consistent advantage. The results indicate that performance depends heavily on the specific backbone and task, suggesting that structural priors in adapters may not be inherently superior to capacity-matched alternatives.

headline_results: Native adapters showed no consistent advantage over token-wise MLPs.
LaBraM performed better with token-wise controls on FACED and TUEV.

key_points: Method study on EEG adaptation: compares native-axis attention adapters that mirror backbone structure against parameter-matched token-wise MLP controls.
Findings show no consistent advantage for native adapters, with token-wise controls performing better on certain tasks such as emotion recognition and event classification.
Highlights the importance of capacity-controlled comparisons when evaluating parameter-efficient tuning strategies for EEG foundation models.
limitations: Results for CBraMod on TUEV may be affected by potential data leakage during pretraining.
The study focuses on adapters placed after a fixed backbone rather than internal tuning like LoRA.
The number of seeds used (3) is small, limiting population-level significance claims.

method.architecture: Native-axis attention adapters (mixing along channel and temporal-patch axes) vs. Token-wise MLP adapters.
method.finetuning: Frozen backbone with trainable adapters and a linear classifier head.
method.objective: Downstream task classification accuracy.
method.pretraining: Uses frozen pretrained EEG-FMs (CBraMod and LaBraM).

summary.unique_contribution: Demonstrates that backbone-informed adapters do not consistently outperform capacity-matched token-wise MLP adapters across different EEG foundation models and downstream tasks.

summary.detailed_summary: PhysioWave-T introduces a foundation model family for biosignals that employs dynamic scale folding to compress multiscale wavelet subbands into a single token sequence, significantly reducing computational overhead. It utilizes route-specific front ends and channel-name embeddings to accommodate varying channel counts and sampling rates within a single Transformer backbone. The EEG encoder, pre-trained on 15M windows, outperforms several existing foundation models across sleep staging and P300 tasks, while the Reliability-aware Latent Fusion (RALF) mechanism improves multimodal seizure detection.

headline_results: Outperforms BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT on 8/9 EEG metrics.
Seizure detection sensitivity increased from 61.4% to 74.4% on SeizeIT2.
Achieved SOTA performance on sEMG and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super.

key_points: New EEG foundation model: A 30M-parameter encoder pre-trained on 15M windows that supports flexible channel counts and sampling rates via route-specific front ends.
Token-efficient architecture: Dynamic scale folding reduces Transformer latency by up to 7.2x and peak memory by up to 12.7x compared to scale expansion.
Multimodal integration: Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) improves seizure detection sensitivity on SeizeIT2 from 61.4% to 74.4% using adaptive weights.
limitations: Requires route-specific front ends for different sampling rates.
Multimodal fusion (RALF) relies on independently pre-trained encoders rather than joint multimodal pre-training.
Performance on very low-channel counts may differ from high-density setups.

method.architecture: Transformer backbone with route-specific wavelet front ends and learned channel-name embeddings.
method.finetuning: Task-specific linear probing and fine-tuning for sleep staging, P300, ERN, and seizure detection.
method.objective: Frequency-guided masked reconstruction.
method.pretraining: Pre-trained on 15M windows of EEG data with varying sampling rates and channel counts.

summary.one_liner: A token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG that uses dynamic scale folding and route-specific front ends to handle diverse acquisition setups.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes ZarrFM, an execution-oriented storage representation that complements BIDS by using a Zarr v3 hierarchy with a two-level consolidated index and canonical channel mapping. Unlike traditional formats like EDF or Parquet, ZarrFM implements block-aligned sharding and an append-only edit protocol to minimize metadata overhead and ensure data integrity. Evaluation on PhysioNet corpora demonstrates significant reductions in storage size and a substantial increase in random-window loading throughput compared to existing formats.

headline_results: 11x faster throughput than Parquet
Metadata queries reduced from 601 to 14
Storage reduced from 42.4 MB/hour to 22.7 MB/hour

key_points: ZarrFM provides a standardized, execution-efficient representation using Zarr v3 to reduce I/O bottlenecks in foundation model pretraining.
Achieves up to 11x faster window sampling than Parquet and reduces metadata queries from 601 to 14 across 200 recordings.
Verified bit-exact readback across 11,877 PhysioNet recordings (8,359 hours), reducing storage from 236.5 GB to approximately 100 GB.
limitations: No end-to-end model training was evaluated to assess the impact on convergence.
Canonical projection is lossy for montages relying on specific references or electrode geometry.
Float-valued sources are quantized, meaning original values are not preserved bit-exactly.
Throughput results confound the storage format with the block-aligned sampler.
Bipolar clinical channels can collide into a single canonical slot, leading to data loss.
The effect of buffer size on optimization dynamics was not evaluated.

method.architecture: Zarr v3 hierarchy with two-level consolidated indexing and canonical channel projection (112 slots).
method.objective: Minimize I/O overhead and standardize EEG data for foundation model pretraining.

summary.one_liner: A Zarr v3-based storage architecture designed to optimize I/O throughput, storage efficiency, and data standardization for large-scale EEG foundation model pretraining.
summary.title: ZarrFM: A Canonical Tensor Storage Architecture for EEG Foundation-Model Pretraining
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a canonical tensor storage architecture for EEG that optimizes the pipeline from raw recordings to model-ready windows via block-aligned sharding and consolidated indexing.

summary.detailed_summary: CABrain introduces a foundation model for EEG decoding that replaces random masking with an adaptive strategy and utilizes Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) for conditional positional encoding. This approach addresses the limitations of treating EEG data as image-like grids by explicitly modeling the spatial correlations between brain channels. The model was pretrained on the TUEG dataset and demonstrated state-of-the-art or competitive performance across ten benchmark datasets.

headline_results: Achieved state-of-the-art or competitive performance across ten benchmark datasets

key_points: New EEG foundation model: CABrain uses GCN-based conditional positional encoding to explicitly model inter-channel correlations.
Implements an adaptive masking strategy to modulate reconstruction difficulty, enhancing the learning of weakly correlated channels.
Demonstrates state-of-the-art or competitive performance across ten benchmark EEG datasets.
limitations: Not explicitly mentioned in the provided text
Potential dependence on the quality of the initial channel correlation estimates

method.architecture: Transformer-based with GCN-based conditional positional encoding
method.finetuning: Finetuned on ten benchmark EEG datasets
method.objective: Masked patch reconstruction
method.pretraining: Pretrained on TUEG dataset using adaptive masking

summary.unique_contribution: The first EEG foundation model to integrate graph-based representations into conditional positional encoding and implement an adaptive masking strategy during pretraining.

summary.detailed_summary: ScaleBrain proposes a pre-training framework that coordinates multi-scale EEG representations by utilizing analysis windows of varying temporal spans with shared temporal anchors. It addresses the gap in prior work by aligning the input tokenization with a scale-specific reconstruction objective, ensuring sufficient supervision across different temporal resolutions. The model incorporates an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism and demonstrates superior performance on six public BCI benchmarks with a compact 5.0M parameter architecture.

headline_results: Highest mean Balanced Accuracy on 5/6 datasets compared to 12 baselines
tasks: BCI benchmarks (e.g., motor imagery, emotion recognition, sleep staging)

key_points: New EEG foundation model: ScaleBrain implements a scale-consistent framework that synchronizes multi-scale input representations with their corresponding self-supervised optimization objectives.
Method novelty: Employs multi-scale tokenization with shared temporal anchors and an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism for efficient feature fusion.
Strong evidence: Outperforms 12 representative baselines on five out of six public BCI benchmarks while utilizing only 5.0M parameters.
limitations: The provided text does not explicitly discuss model limitations.
Evaluation is restricted to six public BCI benchmarks.

method.architecture: Axial spatio-temporal attention, multi-scale tokenization
method.finetuning: Downstream BCI task adaptation
method.objective: Scale-specific reconstruction
method.pretraining: Self-supervised pre-training with scale-consistent reconstruction

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes SeeEEG, a method that renders EEG signals as images (waveforms or scalograms) to be processed by a frozen vision transformer. Unlike existing EEG foundation models that require massive EEG pretraining, SeeEEG optimizes only a lightweight display module (montage, filtering, and contrast) to align EEG patterns with the visual priors of models like DINOv3. Evaluation across eight diverse datasets shows that SeeEEG outperforms seven specialized EEG foundation models in balanced accuracy and mean rank.

headline_results: Outperforms 7 specialized EEG-FMs in balanced accuracy on all 8 datasets
Achieved a mean rank of 1.3 compared to 2.9 for the best EEG-FM (REVE)
tasks: EEG classification across clinical, sleep, affective, and BCI domains

key_points: New method: SeeEEG uses a frozen vision foundation model (e.g., DINOv3) as an EEG encoder by rendering signals as images.
Optimizes a lightweight display module (<= 1,113 parameters) for montage and filtering instead of fine-tuning the backbone.
Outperforms seven specialized EEG foundation models across eight clinical, sleep, affective, and BCI datasets.
limitations: Requires rendering EEG as images, which may introduce computational overhead compared to raw signal processing.
Performance is heavily dependent on the quality and priors of the frozen vision backbone.
The learnable display parameters are optimized per task, potentially limiting zero-shot transfer of the rendering itself.

method.architecture: Frozen DINOv3 ViT-B backbone with a learnable display module (montage, filtering, contrast) that renders EEG as waveforms or scalograms.
method.finetuning: Only the lightweight display module is trained; the ViT backbone remains frozen.
method.objective: Task-specific optimization of display parameters to maximize classification accuracy.
method.pretraining: Uses a frozen vision foundation model pretrained on image data (DINOv3).

summary.unique_contribution: Demonstrates that a frozen vision foundation model, with a learnable rendering module, outperforms specialized EEG foundation models without any EEG-specific pretraining.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a 'resource ladder' (factory → Bayesian head → affine map → full fine-tune) and a clean-referenced mean-shift gate to determine when a deployed BCI decoder should adapt. Unlike typical always-on fine-tuning, this approach uses a utility function to price classification accuracy against computational fit time and label costs. Evidence across five encoder architectures and multiple datasets shows that a lightweight LDA head can recover accuracy under severe synthetic stress at approximately 23x lower fit time than full fine-tuning.

headline_results: LDA head achieved ~23x lower fit time than full fine-tuning while maintaining or improving accuracy under severe stress.

key_points: Method for BCI adaptation: Proposes a resource-priced ladder (factory → Bayesian head → affine map) governed by a regime-aware gate to optimize the cost of adaptation.

Cost-efficient recovery: Demonstrates that a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds frozen trunk accuracy under severe stress across five architectures with ~23x lower fit time than full fine-tuning.
Gated adaptation: Shows that a clean-referenced gate prevents unnecessary adaptation on natural session drift, improving cost-efficiency and safety.
limitations: Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets.
Recovery claims are primarily made under controlled synthetic channel mixing rather than natural drift.
The value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains.

method.architecture: Frozen encoder trunks (e.g., EEGNet, Conformer, ATCNet) with a thin control layer consisting of a Bayesian LDA head or affine map.
method.finetuning: Ladder-based adaptation (L1: Bayesian head update, L2: affine map, L3: full warm-start fine-tuning).
method.objective: Utility maximization: U = acc - lambda_w * t_adapt - mu_n * (n_adapt/N_max).
method.pretraining: Trunks are trained on calibration data and then frozen.

summary.one_liner: A resource-aware adaptation framework for frozen EEG encoders that uses a gated ladder of lightweight heads to balance accuracy, fit time, and label costs.
summary.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a gated, resource-priced adaptation ladder that treats the decision to adapt as a first-class control variable based on a utility trade-off between accuracy, fit time, and label cost.

papers.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), complex-valued temporal filters that function as learnable band-pass filters and a special case of diagonal state-space models. The model is pretrained using a self-supervised objective where the encoder predicts its own future activity via either windowed summaries or dense log-power. Evaluation across four neural benchmarks (TUAB, BrainTreebank, ISRUC-SG1, BCI-IV-2a) shows that the RQF system, with as few as 110k parameters, performs comparably to or better than much larger EEG foundation models.

headline_results: 0.9247 AUROC on TUAB
0.8822 AUROC on BrainTreebank (frozen)
0.8223 balanced accuracy on ISRUC-SG1
0.6108 balanced accuracy on BCI-IV-2a

key_points: New EEG foundation model: A compact RQF encoder using complex-valued temporal filters that explicitly parameterize tuning frequency and bandwidth.
Method novelty: Employs a self-supervised prediction-error objective (windowed or dense) to learn representations without task labels.
Strong evidence: A 110k-parameter model achieves 0.9247 AUROC on TUAB, outperforming SAMBA and rivaling models with up to 369M parameters.
limitations: Most corpora use their own pretrained weights, target geometry, and readout rather than a single universal model.
Cross-corpus transfer was only explicitly tested for the TUEG-to-BCI-IV-2a transition.

method.architecture: Stack of L layers of d complex-valued Recursive Quadrature Filters (diagonal SSMs) with a spatial readout for multichannel fusion.
method.finetuning: Downstream task readouts are trained with the encoder either frozen or fully fine-tuned.
method.objective: Self-supervised future-state prediction using InfoNCE loss (windowed summary prediction or dense log-power prediction).
method.pretraining: Pretrained on unlabeled time series to predict future activity; uses a phase-rotation prior and first-order look-ahead.

summary.one_liner: A compact, biologically motivated RQF encoder using self-supervised future-state prediction to achieve foundation-model performance with orders of magnitude fewer parameters.
summary.title: Self-Supervised Learning with Recursive Quadrature Filters for Neural Time Series
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a highly parameter-efficient EEG encoder based on Recursive Quadrature Filters that leverages biologically motivated oscillatory dynamics and self-supervised future-state prediction.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning with Recursive Quadrature Filters for Neural Time Series

reasons: Develops a self-supervised pretraining framework for EEG and intracranial recordings intended for downstream task readouts.
Evaluates the pretrained representations across four neural benchmarks.
Explicitly frames and compares the model's performance and efficiency against existing EEG foundation models.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper investigates claims by Dani and Liebe (2026) that SSL adaptation of the final encoder block in BIOT and CBraMod significantly boosts seizure detection performance. The authors identify critical implementation errors in the original release, including the use of random initialization instead of pretrained weights and active dropout during probing. After correcting these issues and applying a revised protocol with subject rotations on CHB-MIT and Siena Scalp EEG, the reported gains are found to be negligible or non-existent, suggesting the original results were artifacts of implementation bugs.

headline_results: BIOT adaptation gain reduced from 36.2 to -0.6 ROC-AUC
CBraMod adaptation gain reduced from 29.5 to +0.01 ROC-AUC

key_points: Benchmark audit: Investigates the reproducibility of SSL adaptation gains for BIOT and CBraMod on seizure detection.
Identifies critical bugs in the original release, such as random weight initialization during adaptation and active dropout during probing.
Shows that corrected evaluation on CHB-MIT and Siena datasets reduces reported ROC-AUC gains from ~30 points to near zero.
limitations: Findings are specific to the tested configurations and the encoder-level probe chosen post hoc.
The +/- 3 point margin used for equivalence is an analysis threshold, not a clinically validated one.
Some comparisons (6 of 18) remained unresolved.

method.architecture: Linear probing and SSL adaptation of BIOT and CBraMod encoder blocks
method.finetuning: SSL adaptation of the final encoder block followed by linear probing
method.objective: Seizure detection (binary classification)
method.pretraining: Pretrained BIOT and CBraMod encoders

summary.one_liner: An audit of SSL adaptation gains for BIOT and CBraMod on CHB-MIT, finding that reported improvements vanish when using pretrained weights and proper evaluation modes.
summary.title: Large Reported CHB-MIT Adaptation Gains Disappear with Pretrained Encoders and Matched Probes
summary.unique_contribution: Demonstrates that large reported SSL adaptation gains for EEG foundation models on CHB-MIT were artifacts of implementation errors and an inadequate evaluation protocol.

papers.title: Large Reported CHB-MIT Adaptation Gains Disappear with Pretrained Encoders and Matched Probes

reasons: Focuses on the evaluation and adaptation of specific EEG foundation models (BIOT and CBraMod)
Analyzes the effectiveness of self-supervised learning (SSL) adaptation for pretrained EEG representations
Provides a critical audit of adaptation gains and probing protocols for EEG-FMs

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes the Mind World Model (MWM), which jointly trains a mind model to encode EEG and a world model to predict future visual frames from egocentric video. Unlike prior work relying on cue-based trials or EEG-only self-supervision, MWM uses a movement-grounded objective that aligns neural activity with the visual consequences of behavior. The approach incorporates a Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT) to handle hemispheric symmetry and is evaluated across 16 motor decoding tasks, showing significant improvements in accuracy and correlation.

headline_results: Balanced accuracy improved by 5.9%
Pearson correlation improved by 16.2%

key_points: New EEG foundation model: MWM learns motor representations by predicting the visual consequences of behavior using synchronized EEG and egocentric video.
Introduces the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT) to explicitly separate bilateral and lateral EEG features, improving hemispheric correspondence.
Demonstrates superior performance across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, improving balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2%.
limitations: Reliance on synchronized egocentric video and EEG data, which may be difficult to collect at massive scales.
The world model's ability to generalize to entirely different environments beyond the EgoBrain dataset is not extensively detailed.
Performance gains are measured via linear probing, which may not capture the full potential of the representations.

method.architecture: Mind Model (EEG encoder) and World Model (visual predictor) utilizing a Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT).
method.finetuning: Linear probing on downstream motor classification and regression tasks.
method.objective: Predict the representation of a future visual frame given EEG observed up to the current frame.
method.pretraining: Joint learning on synchronized EEG and egocentric video without action labels.

summary.one_liner: A framework that learns motor EEG representations by treating EEG as a latent action to predict future egocentric visual states.
summary.title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a pretraining objective that treats EEG as a latent action for predicting future visual states in egocentric video, eliminating the need for explicit action annotations.

papers.title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics

reasons: Learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video
Uses a pretraining objective to create a mind model for downstream motor decoding
Evaluated across a broad set of 9 classification and 7 regression tasks
Explicitly targets the creation of transferable motor representations

summary.detailed_summary: LingSante-Pulse proposes a shared, signal-conditioned encoder that processes multiple physiological modalities independently to support both multimodal and single-sensor inference. It introduces a joint pretraining objective combining pairwise cross-modal alignment, structured random-feature prediction (RFP), and masked waveform reconstruction to capture both inter-signal relationships and intra-signal structures. The model was evaluated across 38 tasks, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance with a frozen encoder in domains including EEG sleep staging (0.7941 Macro-F1) and ECG apnea screening (0.9183 AUROC).

headline_results: Sleep-EDF EEG-only staging: Macro-F1 0.7941
Apnea-ECG single-lead: AUROC 0.9183
HMC multimodal sleep staging: Macro-F1 0.7784
EEGMMIDB 64-channel motor imagery: Macro-F1 0.5150

key_points: New EEG foundation model: A unified framework (LingSante-Pulse) that learns shared representations across EEG, ECG, PPG, and EMG using a single signal-conditioned encoder.
Novel pretraining: Combines masked reconstruction with structured random-feature prediction and pairwise alignment to preserve rhythmic information and enable transitive transfer between modalities.
Strong evidence: Achieves top mean ranks across 38 tasks, including high performance in EEG-only sleep staging (0.7941 Macro-F1) and single-lead ECG apnea screening (0.9183 AUROC).
limitations: Reliance on the availability of synchronized multi-modal pairs for cross-modal alignment pretraining.
Potential sensitivity to the choice of random teacher functions used in the Random-Feature Prediction objective.

method.architecture: Shared signal-conditioned encoder
method.finetuning: Evaluated using a frozen encoder with linear readouts or BiLSTM heads
method.objective: Joint objective of pairwise cross-modal alignment, structured random-feature prediction (RFP), and masked waveform reconstruction
method.pretraining: Pretrained on heterogeneous physiological recordings using random teacher functions for RFP and synchronized pairs for alignment

summary.one_liner: A unified physiological representation framework using random-feature prediction and cross-modal alignment to learn reusable features across EEG, ECG, PPG, and EMG.
summary.title: LingSante-Pulse: Unified Physiological Pretraining through Random-Feature Prediction and Cross-Modal Alignment
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a unified encoder that enables transitive relational bridging across partially overlapping physiological recordings through a combination of random-feature prediction and cross-modal alignment.

papers.title: LingSante-Pulse: Unified Physiological Pretraining through Random-Feature Prediction and Cross-Modal Alignment

reasons: Proposes a unified, general-purpose physiological representation framework that explicitly includes EEG as a core modality.
Uses pretraining (random-feature prediction and masked reconstruction) to learn reusable features across signal types.
Evaluates a frozen encoder across 38 tasks, including EEG-only sleep staging, demonstrating broad transferability.

datasets: Temple University Hospital Seizure Corpus (TUSZ v2.0.3)

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes an open-set recognition (OSR) framework for EEG seizure type classification, moving beyond the standard closed-set assumption. It defines known and unknown classes based on subject representation in the TUSZ v2.0.3 dataset and evaluates seven post-hoc scorers applied to a fine-tuned EEG Foundation Model. Results show that while some scorers achieve a mean AUROC of 0.66 for unknown classes, detecting held-out known types from unseen subjects remains near chance, highlighting the difficulty of the task.

headline_results: Best scorer (Mahalanobis) achieved mean AUROC of 0.66 on true unknown classes
Held-out knowns AUROC 0.54-0.58

key_points: Benchmark protocol: Introduces the first open-set recognition framework for EEG seizure type classification on the TUSZ v2.0.3 corpus.
Methodological evaluation: Tests seven post-hoc OSR scorers on a fine-tuned EEG foundation model using a subject-disjoint leave-one-class-out protocol.
Performance findings: Demonstrates that open-set seizure recognition is challenging, with the best scorer reaching 0.66 AUROC for unknown classes.
limitations: Open-set seizure type recognition remains a hard, open problem with low AUROC.
Detection of held-out known seizure types from unseen subjects is only slightly above chance.
Per-subject rejection rates are highly uneven across all tested scorers.
GHOST does not significantly improve per-subject fairness over energy scoring.

method.architecture: EEG Foundation Model (EFM) with post-hoc open-set scorers (MSP, MaxLogit, energy, Mahalanobis, kNN, GHOST, COSTARR)
method.finetuning: Partially fine-tuned on known seizure types
method.objective: Seizure type classification / Open-set recognition
method.pretraining: Pretrained EEG foundation model

summary.one_liner: Introduces the first open-set recognition benchmark for EEG seizure type classification using a fine-tuned EEG foundation model.
summary.title: A Benchmark Protocol and Fairness Analysis Towards Open-Set EEG Seizure Type Classification
summary.unique_contribution: Establishes a clinically-grounded open-set recognition protocol for EEG seizure classification on the TUSZ corpus to evaluate the ability of models to reject rare or atypical seizure types.

papers.title: A Benchmark Protocol and Fairness Analysis Towards Open-Set EEG Seizure Type Classification

reasons: EEG is the central modality of the study.
The paper explicitly evaluates a 'partially fine-tuned EEG Foundation Model (EFM)'.
It proposes a benchmark protocol and evaluation for open-set recognition using an EEG-FM.

papers.title: PhyMind: Physics-Informed Masked Autoencoding for EEG Foundation Models

reasons: Title and abstract explicitly frame the work as being for 'EEG Foundation Models'.
Proposes a new pre-training architecture (physics-informed masked autoencoding) to create reusable EEG representations.
Evaluates the model on downstream tasks and compares performance against an existing EEG-FM (MANAS-2).
Pre-trained on a large-scale dataset of 3k hours of open EEG.

summary.detailed_summary: SleepXA proposes a compositional framework that integrates pretrained neural and cardiac foundation models instead of training a multimodal sleep model from scratch. It employs sleep-guided alignment to separate shared common representations from modality-specific information through common-space alignment, private-space preservation, and common-specific disentanglement. The model was pretrained on 9,230 overnight PSG recordings and evaluated on 27 downstream tasks, demonstrating superior performance in sleep staging, clinical prediction, and daytime physiological transfer, outperforming models trained from scratch.

headline_results: Ranks top two on 22/27 tasks
Ranks first on 17/27 tasks

key_points: Composes pretrained EEG and ECG foundation models with lightweight encoders for other PSG modalities to learn robust sleep representations.
Utilizes a three-module alignment strategy (common-space, private-space, and disentanglement) to preserve modality-specific knowledge while learning shared features.
Achieved top-two performance on 22 of 27 downstream tasks across 15 datasets, including clinical and non-sleep physiological transfer.
limitations: Requires synchronized multimodal PSG data for the composition phase.
Dependence on the quality and availability of independently pretrained modality-specific foundation models.
Potential challenges in scaling to modalities without existing foundation models.

method.architecture: Composition of pretrained EEG and ECG foundation models with lightweight encoders for other PSG modalities.
method.finetuning: Evaluated on 27 downstream tasks across 15 datasets.
method.objective: Sleep-guided alignment involving common-space alignment, modality-specific preservation, and common-specific disentanglement using contrastive and structural losses.
method.pretraining: Pretrained on 9,230 overnight PSG recordings.

summary.one_liner: A framework that composes independently pretrained EEG and ECG foundation models using synchronized PSG data to learn versatile sleep representations.
summary.title: SleepXA: Composing Pretrained Neural and Cardiac Foundation Models for Sleep Representation Learning
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a compositional paradigm that leverages existing modality-specific foundation models via synchronized multimodal physiology as a natural interface for alignment.

papers.title: SleepXA: Composing Pretrained Neural and Cardiac Foundation Models for Sleep Representation Learning

reasons: Explicitly utilizes and composes existing pretrained EEG foundation models.
Develops a multimodal foundation model (SleepXA) with EEG as a core target modality.
Demonstrates broad transferability across 27 downstream tasks and daytime physiological settings.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a systematic framework to disentangle the effects of readout mechanisms (pooling) from layer depth in frozen EEG foundation models. It demonstrates that while optimizing the readout recovers much of the final layer's performance, intermediate layers still provide unique predictive utility. The authors provide evidence across five models and multiple tasks that layer-readout interfaces selected on source datasets transfer effectively to target datasets, reducing the need for target-side search.

headline_results: Source-selected interfaces outperformed final-layer baselines in 10/10 cross-dataset comparisons for CBraMod and REVE.

key_points: Method for EEG-FM interfacing: Proposes a sequential selection process to optimize readout and depth for frozen feature extraction.
Depth vs. Readout: Finds that intermediate layers maintain a predictive advantage even after the final-layer readout is optimized.
Cross-dataset transfer: Shows that interfaces selected on source data outperform final-layer baselines on target datasets across various EEG tasks.
limitations: Analysis is limited to frozen feature extraction rather than full fine-tuning.
The number of evaluated readout families is relatively small.
Cross-dataset transfer was tested on a limited number of dataset pairs.
Residual utility analysis depends on the choice of PCA dimensionality.

method.architecture: Frozen feature extraction from five EEG-FMs (CBraMod, REVE, LaBraM, LUNA, CSBrain) using a sequential selection of readout and layer depth.
method.finetuning: Frozen backbone with linear readout probes.
method.objective: Linear probing for downstream task performance and PCA-based residual analysis for predictive utility.
method.pretraining: Analyzes existing pre-trained foundation models.

summary.one_liner: Investigates the impact of readout mechanisms and layer depth on the predictive utility of frozen EEG foundation models and their transferability across datasets.
summary.title: Layer-Readout Interfaces in EEG Foundation Models: Predictive Accessibility and Cross-Dataset Transfer
summary.unique_contribution: Demonstrates that source-selected layer-readout interfaces provide a reusable and transferable feature interface across different EEG datasets.

papers.title: Layer-Readout Interfaces in EEG Foundation Models: Predictive Accessibility and Cross-Dataset Transfer

reasons: Explicitly focuses on 'EEG foundation models' in both title and abstract.
Investigates the use of these models as frozen feature extractors for cross-dataset transfer.
Analyzes the predictive utility and depth structure of representations across multiple EEG-FMs and tasks.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a framework for EEG decoding based on in-context learning (ICL), utilizing a frozen general-purpose predictor instead of traditional task-specific fine-tuning. It introduces EEG-specific context construction—incorporating waveform, spectral, covariance, regional, and local-temporal representations—alongside a metric-based adaptation mechanism to select the optimal context without requiring validation data. The approach was evaluated across ten datasets and seven paradigms, achieving the highest mean BAcc compared to eleven specialized and fine-tuned baselines.

headline_results: Achieved highest mean BAcc compared to 11 specialized and fine-tuned baselines.

key_points: New EEG decoding method: utilizes a frozen general-purpose in-context predictor to perform tuning-free decoding by treating labeled examples as context.
Develops diverse context construction strategies (spectral, covariance, regional, etc.) and a support-only metric for automatic context selection.
Outperforms eleven specialized and fine-tuned baselines across ten datasets and seven EEG paradigms in mean BAcc.
limitations: Deployment cost increases with wider waveform features and multiview contexts.
Requires multiple prediction passes for One-vs-Rest (OVR) configurations.
Raw vectorization is unstable and does not generalize reliably across paradigms without specialized context construction.

method.architecture: Frozen general-purpose ICL predictor (e.g., TabPFN/TabICL) with EEG-specific context construction.
method.finetuning: Tuning-free; adaptation occurs via context construction and metric-based selection.
method.objective: In-context learning for classification/regression without parameter updates.
method.pretraining: Uses a pre-trained general-purpose tabular ICL model.

summary.one_liner: A tuning-free EEG decoding framework that leverages in-context learning and specialized context construction to avoid parameter updates during deployment.
summary.title: EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a tuning-free EEG foundation model paradigm where task adaptation is achieved through EEG-specific context construction and a metric-based selection rule rather than gradient-based parameter updates.

papers.title: EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models

reasons: Explicitly proposes a framework for 'tuning-free EEG foundation models'.
Develops a foundation-model paradigm based on in-context learning for EEG decoding.
Evaluates the approach across ten datasets and seven EEG decoding paradigms to demonstrate broad transferability.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes EEGJev, a model that combines a frozen CBraMod EEG encoder and a frozen MPNet text encoder via a bidirectional Transformer decision head to score candidate answers. Unlike prior work that uses task-specific heads, EEGJev handles multiple attributes through a question-answering interface. The authors introduce EEGJev-Bench, covering six question types across 19 public datasets, demonstrating that the model follows questions with 99.7% accuracy and achieves D1 balanced accuracy (63.8%) comparable to task-specific EEGNet.

headline_results: 63.8% balanced accuracy on D1 (vs 64.5% EEGNet)
99.7% attribute selection accuracy

key_points: New EEG foundation model and benchmark: EEGJev enables multi-task EEG decoding by scoring candidate answers based on natural language questions.
Architecture uses a frozen CBraMod EEG encoder and MPNet text encoder joined by a 2-layer bidirectional Transformer decision head.
Demonstrates high question-following reliability (99.7% accuracy) and competitive performance against task-specific models across 19 public EEG sources.
limitations: Performance on specific answers (62.04% BA) is lower than the ability to simply identify the correct attribute (99.7%).
D2 joint scores (both questions correct) are significantly lower than individual question scores.
T2 long-window timing accuracy is relatively low (15% for EEGJev).
Performance drops when using held-out phrasings (D1h).

method.architecture: CBraMod EEG encoder + MPNet text encoder + 2-layer bidirectional Transformer decision head + Act head for refusal.
method.finetuning: Decision head and Act head are trained on EEGJev-Bench.
method.objective: Scoring candidate answers via softmax over offered options.
method.pretraining: CBraMod is pretrained; then fine-tuned on 19 sources and frozen.

summary.one_liner: A question-guided EEG decision model and benchmark designed to evaluate multi-task decoding and question-following capabilities.
summary.title: EEGJev: A System One Decision Model and Benchmark for Multi-Task EEG Question Answering
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a single-pass decision model that can switch decoding targets for the same EEG recording simply by changing the input question.

papers.title: EEGJev: A System One Decision Model and Benchmark for Multi-Task EEG Question Answering

reasons: Explicitly mentions EEG foundation models and the need to evaluate how they handle changing questions.
Introduces EEGJev-Bench, a benchmark specifically designed to test EEG decoders/foundation models across 19 public sources.
Compares performance against NeuroLM, an existing EEG foundation model.

summary.detailed_summary: The paper proposes EEG-World, a recurrent world model designed to forecast 10 seconds of EEG band-power dynamics using 6 seconds of prior EEG and subsequent audiovisual input. Unlike traditional encoding models that ignore the viewer's current brain state, EEG-World learns shared neural dynamics pretrained on continuous EEG and adapts to individuals via lightweight readouts. Using 2,584 hours of EEG from 78 participants, the model demonstrates superior forecasting correlation (0.261) and a longer forecasting horizon compared to strong history-aware linear baselines.

headline_results: Forecasting correlation of 0.261 vs 0.233 for linear baselines
3.3-second increase in forecasting horizon
Outperformed linear baselines in 23/24 unseen subjects
tasks: Zero-shot and calibrated transfer to unseen subjects

key_points: New EEG foundation model: A recurrent world model that predicts future EEG band-power by integrating preceding neural history with audiovisual stimuli.
Demonstrates that nonlinear recurrent forecasting outperforms history-aware linear baselines at scale, achieving a 3.3-second advantage in forecasting horizon.
Shows strong transferability to unseen participants, outperforming linear baselines in 23 out of 24 individuals after calibration.
limitations: Reliance on large-scale datasets to outperform linear baselines.
Zero-shot transfer performance was lower than pooled linear models.
Some hypothesis tests regarding persistence-controlled identification failed to reach significance.
Audio features provided smaller gains compared to visual features.

method.architecture: Recurrent world model with a recurrent dynamics core and lightweight subject-specific readouts.
method.finetuning: Lightweight calibration of subject-specific readouts for unseen individuals.
method.objective: Forecasting 10 seconds of EEG band-power dynamics.
method.pretraining: Pretrained on continuous EEG data to learn shared neural dynamics.

summary.one_liner: A recurrent world model that forecasts individual EEG band-power dynamics by conditioning on both preceding neural activity and audiovisual stimuli.
summary.title: EEG-World: Context-Conditioned Dynamics of the Watching Brain
summary.unique_contribution: Introduces a recurrent world model that separates state-driven from stimulus-driven predictability to forecast individualized EEG trajectories.

papers.title: EEG-World: Context-Conditioned Dynamics of the Watching Brain

reasons: Pretrained on a large-scale dataset (2,584 hours of EEG) to learn shared neural dynamics.
Explicitly focuses on transferable representations that adapt to unseen individuals via lightweight readouts.
Frames the work as a 'recurrent world model' for general EEG band-power forecasting.
